record.title: A mathematical-analysis preprint reports mismatches between OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes proof and cited Lean estimates
record.summary: Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen compare OpenAI’s natural-language Navier–Stokes proof with cited Lean declarations. For Lemma 8.6, equation (8.19), they report that the manuscript states an m+4 derivative estimate while the cited Lean estimate requires m+5. For pressure-flux equation (10.19), they report a different Lean bound and proof route, including an additional localized gradient norm. Static inspection of the pinned source shows a related canonical cutoff-flux bound is used along the option-C proof path; whether it is equivalent or sufficient for the manuscript argument remains unresolved. The authors do not claim the natural-language blow-up proof is incorrect. The critique remains an author-reported result without independent reproduction or established specialist consensus. A later auditor-authored red-team report claims pinned build and semantic-bridge checks and reports no material discrepancy falsifying the formal chain; the research desk inspected the report but did not reproduce its checks, and its claims do not settle the natural-language proof or Clay review.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors compare OpenAI’s natural-language proof of Lemma 8.6, equation (8.19), with its cited Lean declaration at commit f9e8bc5. They report the manuscript estimate uses m+4 input derivatives while the cited Lean estimate requires m+5; this is a concrete mismatch in the stated bound, not a demonstration that the Navier–Stokes blow-up theorem is false.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report a different Lean pressure-flux bound and proof route from manuscript equation (10.19), including a localized gradient norm. Static inspection at the cited OpenAI commit f9e8bc5 also finds a related canonical cutoff-flux bound on the option-C proof path. This establishes a code-path connection, not equivalence or sufficiency of the Lean inequality for the manuscript argument.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors argue that Lean acceptance verifies the encoded formal statement, not semantic preservation of the natural-language proof. They explicitly disclaim making a claim about whether OpenAI’s natural-language proof is correct.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: At the pinned source revision, option C calls theorem_1_1; its no-global-solution step depends on whole-space uniqueness, which invokes exists_uniform_actual_pressure_flux_bound and then exists_uniform_canonicalCutoffFlux_bound. The code path therefore uses a related cutoff-flux bound, while whether it proves the manuscript’s equation (10.19) or supplies an equivalent argument remains unresolved.

contradictory_evidence: An independent audit report says it pinned OpenAI source 8937a8f4cbc7abaab5e9e97d1cc7f5d2319d9538, Lean v4.34.0-rc2, Mathlib 85e3a25e and Comparator 19e111; it reports an 11,251-job build, a live Comparator rerun using reused/replayed Lake artifacts, and a separate ClaySpec-to-Comparator correspondence check, concluding it found no material discrepancy capable of falsifying the formal chain. The report also corrects two provenance claims in its earlier audit and retains human interpretation boundaries. This self-published report qualifies the earlier mismatch critique but does not independently settle the estimates, prove the natural-language argument, or establish Clay acceptance; the research desk did not reproduce its checks. evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of the reported m+4/m+5 or pressure-flux estimate comparisons, proof of equivalence between the code-path cutoff-flux bound and manuscript equation (10.19), or reconciliation against later OpenAI repository revisions has been completed.

The critique does not refute the underlying blow-up theorem. Static inspection traces a related canonical cutoff-flux bound into the option-C proof path, but whether that bound is sufficient or semantically equivalent to manuscript equation (10.19) remains unresolved; the derivative-order mismatch and complete theorem-level implications also need expert assessment.

A current auditor-authored red-team report claims a pinned build, Comparator rerun and ClaySpec correspondence check, but the research desk has not reproduced those checks or independently assessed the audit methodology; it does not establish natural-language proof fidelity, specialist consensus or Clay adjudication.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported mismatches hold, a machine-checked Lean result cannot be treated as verification of the specific natural-language proof without a semantic bridge. This changes how an extraordinary mathematical claim should be evaluated, although the audit does not refute the underlying theorem.
limitations: This is an author-reported analysis in an arXiv v1 preprint; peer review and independent specialist consensus were not established.
The paper compares selected proof components and cited Lean declarations; it does not establish that the underlying Navier–Stokes blow-up theorem is false.

For pressure-flux equation (10.19), the authors report a different bound involving localized gradient norm A_R. Static inspection places a related canonical cutoff-flux bound on the option-C proof path, but does not show that the two arguments are equivalent or that the Lean inequality is insufficient.
No independent reproduction, Lean build, proof of estimate equivalence, or audit of later upstream revisions was performed.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report an m+4 versus m+5 derivative requirement in Lemma 8.6 and a distinct pressure-flux estimate/proof route for equation (10.19), challenging correspondence between selected manuscript arguments and cited Lean declarations.
technical.demonstrated_result: The cited primary preprint and pinned code are accessible. Static source inspection traces a related canonical cutoff-flux bound into the option-C theorem path. the research desk did not independently reproduce the estimates, prove equivalence to the manuscript argument, or run Lean; the underlying theorem is not refuted by this inspection.
technical.implementation_status: Mathematical-analysis preprint arXiv v1; no independent reproduction by this research run.
technical.mechanism: Compares selected estimates and proof steps in OpenAI’s natural-language Navier–Stokes paper against cited Lean declarations and pinned source revisions. The critique separates encoded theorem validity from semantic fidelity to the written argument.
technical.regime: Selected analytic estimates in one natural-language Navier–Stokes proof and corresponding Lean declarations at pinned revision f9e8bc5; static inspection traces a related cutoff-flux bound to option C but does not settle semantic fidelity or theorem correctness.
technical.reproducibility: The paper cites exact manuscript sections and Lean revisions; the research desk re-read these and statically traced the pressure-flux dependency at f9e8bc5 but did not independently derive the estimates, establish equivalence, or build/check Lean. technical.strongest_baseline: OpenAI’s natural-language paper and its cited Lean declarations are compared directly. A current auditor-authored report provides counterevidence to a broad claim that the formal chain contains a material falsifying discrepancy, while leaving independent reproduction and natural-language semantic fidelity unresolved.

brief.title: A mathematical-analysis preprint reports mismatches between OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes proof and cited Lean estimates
brief.why_it_matters: A formal proof establishes its encoded theorem, but it does not by itself establish that the theorem matches the natural-language argument it is meant to check. The reported estimate differences give concrete targets for independent Lean and PDE review of an extraordinary mathematical claim, while leaving the truth of the underlying blow-up result unresolved.
